interest: This file provides valuable documentary evidence of Axis commercial ties and blockade-running logistics during the period of the Soviet-German non-aggression pact, illustrating how German interests utilized the Trans-Siberian Railway to obtain agricultural goods from Japan despite exorbitant rail freight rates and British contraband seizures. It also offers economic and legal historians an exceptionally thorough primary source in English on the administrative machinery of Japan's state tobacco monopoly, detailing how Meiji-era fiscal monopolies regulated domestic cultivation, enforced compulsory delivery and grading, and structured trade exceptions for Japanese colonial territories through the interwar period.
overview: This file contains U.S. State Department records from 1940 and 1941 concerning the Japanese tobacco industry, state monopoly controls, and wartime commerce. It consists of a confidential voluntary consular report from April 1940 by American Vice Consul W. Garland Richardson in Tokyo detailing a contract negotiated by Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha for the Imperial Monopoly Bureau to sell 200,000 kilograms of leaf tobacco to German interests via Vladivostok and the Trans-Siberian Railway following British interception of an earlier maritime shipment, alongside a May 1941 diplomatic despatch from First Secretary George A. Makinson enclosing a complete English translation prepared by the Canadian Legation of Japan's 1904 Tobacco Monopoly Law and its Finance Department operational regulations.

subfiles.about: Reports on a commercial contract for the sale of Japanese leaf tobacco to German interests and the logistics of its overland transit across Siberia.
subfiles.summary: American Vice Consul W. Garland Richardson reports on an April 19, 1940 contract signed by Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha on behalf of the Imperial Monopoly Bureau to sell 200,000 kilograms of leaf tobacco to Germany at RM 1.00 per kilogram with delivery in Japan. An earlier August 1939 contract for 2,000,000 kilograms had been cancelled after the initial shipment was captured and confiscated by British naval forces following the outbreak of war in Europe. Due to rail freight charges twelve times higher than pre-war maritime shipping and uncertain transit times, the Monopoly refused to deliver to Germany or guarantee delivery to Vladivostok, requiring German buyers to accept delivery in Japan and repack hogsheads into 100-kilogram bales for rail transport. A representative of the British-American Tobacco Company attached to the Monopoly observed that Germany's willingness to commit approximately twenty rail cars to tobacco suggested it was experiencing little difficulty securing Trans-Siberian transport for military supplies.
subfiles.title: Report on Sale of Leaf Tobacco to German Interests by the Japanese Tobacco Monopoly

subfiles.about: Transmits an English translation of the Japanese Tobacco Monopoly Law and regulations as background reference for U.S. government agencies.

subfiles.summary: First Secretary of Embassy George A. Makinson forwards to Secretary of State Cordell Hull a complete English translation of the Japanese Tobacco Monopoly Law incorporating all amendments. Prepared by the Canadian Legation in Tokyo, the legislation had seen no recent alterations but was transmitted as useful background reference material for the Department of Agriculture and the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5570 Transmitting Translation of Japanese Tobacco Monopoly Law

subfiles.about: Presents the complete translated text of Japan's Tobacco Monopoly Law of 1904 and its detailed administrative enforcement regulations.
subfiles.summary: This enclosure provides the full English translation of the Japanese Tobacco Monopoly Law (Law No. 14 of 1904, amended through 1925) and its accompanying Finance Department enforcement regulations (Ordinance No. 19 of 1904, amended through 1923). The statutory system establishes an exclusive government monopoly over tobacco manufacturing, importation, and distribution, closely regulating private growers through permits, acreage restrictions, seedbed supervision, and compulsory crop delivery with official quality assessment. It details rules for wholesale and retail licensing, export procedures including special terms for Japanese colonies, indemnification schemes and state treasury notes for former private manufacturers, and penal sanctions for unauthorized cultivation, manufacturing, or contraband sales.
subfiles.title: Translation of the Japanese Tobacco Monopoly Law and Enforcement Regulations
